criteria.criterion: Grep of docs/spec.toml shows every active [[requirement]] (135 entries today) carries mechanism, owner and measure; where nothing meets one, mechanism is the literal "none". The measure names where it appears in athena status.
criteria.evidence: Read docs/spec.toml with the Grep tool: requirements carry mechanism/owner/measure lines, and 23 have mechanism = "none" (e.g. OLY-1-07, OLY-2-07, OLY-A-07), each with an owner and a measure ending in `status: <label>`. In the spec test, every_active_requirement_has_a_mechanism_an_owner_and_a_measure passed (it requires at least 135 active requirements) and printed the 23 ids whose mechanism is none. In hestia, the_real_spec_records_every_field_and_classes_the_acceleration_requirements_as_speed passed: it parses the real file and checks that every active measure has a known status label or `not shown` (at least 137 active requirements).

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p xtask --test spec`: it passes on docs/spec.toml, and new in-memory negative cases fail an active requirement missing mechanism, owner or measure.
criteria.evidence: 26 passed, 0 failed. the_real_spec_passes is ok. an_active_requirement_missing_mechanism_owner_or_measure_fails covers 7 damage cases: cleared mechanism, cleared owner, owner none, cleared measure, measure None, a measure with no label, and an empty label. Each asserts an error that names the id and the field, and that a superseded requirement is exempt. Requirement gains #[serde(default)] fields, so a missing field is reported as a check error rather than a parse error.

A requirement about speed gets an urgent request (OP-23). A failing measure is also flagged.

The second run queues 0 with already_open 1, the review_passes line reports this, the run after close queues 1, and once the spec is fixed it queues 0. a_speed_requirement_is_urgent_and_a_statement_with_faster_is_not_enough shows throughput and checks measures queued as urgent while a statement that merely says 'faster' stays normal. a_failing_measure_is_flagged... shows an unknown label is queued as 'a valid measure', while `not shown`, superseded requirements and a missing spec queue nothing. spec_request calls StewardRequest::new (hestia.rs:586).

findings.summary: Whether a requirement counts as being about speed comes from its measure label (throughput or checks), not from a field of its own. A speed requirement whose measure says 'status: not shown' would be queued at normal priority.
findings.evidence: is_speed reads SPEED_LABELS = ["throughput", "checks"] from the measure label. Using the label avoids false positives from keywords, and a test covers that. But urgency then depends on the measure the author chose. An explicit field such as `speed = true`, or a kind, would state it directly.

findings.summary: On the real repository, athena status will gain about 23 next-step lines, one for each requirement whose mechanism is none.
findings.evidence: The spec test output lists 23 requirements with mechanism none. Status pushes one next line per gap and has no cap or summary line, unlike the queue's five-per-pass cap. This is an estimate from the spec content; I did not run status on the real repository.

findings.summary: Two new requirements were added, and two brief headings that fall after the spec test's cutoff date (PINNED_HEADINGS) can be cited again. This goes beyond 'fill the new fields for the existing requirements'.
findings.evidence: OLY-A-22 and OLY-A-23 did not exist in the base spec. Adding them was needed so the acceleration requirement could record a mechanism (criterion 7). The critic accepted this in the plan, and the change stays within the listed files. The source quotes of existing requirements are unchanged.

summary: The change does what the request asks. Every active requirement in docs/spec.toml now has a mechanism, an owner and a measure. Where nothing meets a requirement, the mechanism is the literal "none" (23 requirements, listed by the spec test's output). Each measure ends with `status: <label>` or `status: not shown`. The spec test fails when any of the three fields is missing, and superseded requirements are exempt. Hestia gets a new pass, `Athena::spec_review`, which runs in every drain and sweep. It builds its requests with the shared StewardRequest builder and queues one request per gap (a mechanism of none, or a measure that is blank or names a status line that does not exist). It queues nothing more while that request is open, and asks again after the request is closed. A request is urgent when the requirement's measure is shown under throughput or checks, and one pass queues at most five. `athena status` lists the same gaps in its next-step lines, giving the reason and the owner for each. The CHANGELOG has an entry. I ran the spec test, the athena-core hestia tests and the athena-core status tests, and all passed. fmt, clippy and the full test suite passed in Athena's recorded checks. All findings are minor or nits: the speed rule depends on the measure label; on the real repository, status will gain about 23 next-step lines; and two new requirements (OLY-A-22, OLY-A-23) were added, with two brief headings that fall after the spec test's cutoff date made citable again. The new requirements were needed so the acceleration requirement could be recorded at all.
